children: By Erin Mulvaney and Rosie Ettenheim

The demise of Weil, Gotshal & Manges stunned people across the legal industry and beyond. While the dissolution of a respected 95-year-old law firm was an extreme outlier event, the forces that led to it aren't.

A profession once marked by stability and predictability is more volatile than it has ever been. This year, a record number of partners left the top 100 largest firms by revenue. That figure is on track this year for a nearly 100% increase from just over a decade ago.

The cutthroat jockeying for talent helped bring down Weil Gotshal, which saw a string of high-profile partner departures in recent months and divisive internal debates about whether the firm should scale up to compete with industry leaders or maintain its tightknit internal culture. That has put many other law firms — including decades-old New York institutions and firms that are large but not giant — on guard.
Here are the numbers behind an industry in turmoil — focusing on some of the most high-profile names — and how that turbulence brought down a firm that once seemed untouchable.
Decade of feuding

The bare-knuckled competition over talent has been a decade in the making. Changes in compensation models mean that partners for the most part are no longer paid in line with seniority, allowing firms to raid each other for rainmakers. The going rate for top talent is in the $20 million to $30 million range annually, not counting bonuses. Companies are also less loyal to just one firm and are willing to follow partners with whom they have relationships.

The data on law firm exits, tracked by SurePoint Technologies, includes retirements and departures for in-house corporate jobs. The company scrapes law-firm websites for new hires and announcements to track head counts and lawyer moves.
Numbers game

The financial driver behind the outsize compensation packages is the skyrocketing fees firms have been able to charge for corporate dealmaking, including private equity and mergers-and-acquisitions work. The rapidly growing private-equity industry in particular is a revenue generator because clients require constant advice on a high volume of complicated deals.

Many corporate clients have gravitated to large global firms that can meet all their legal needs. These firms have been able to rake in ever-higher revenue and profits, and in turn use those earnings to lure more top partners and their clients.

There are exceptions: Wachtell is the most profitable law firm in the world and has stayed intentionally small. But it has also been hit with high-profile partner defections, including that of its co-chair earlier this year, that have called its model into question.
Rise of the megafirm
Driving the changes in the industry is the rise of megafirms, corporate-law behemoths with thousands of lawyers and revenue that rivals Fortune 500 companies.

Two firms in particular dominate: Kirkland & Ellis and Latham & Watkins. Over the past decade or so, the firms, with roots in Chicago and Los Angeles, respectively, have transformed from dominant national players into global powerhouses.

Many other places are now trying to emulate Kirkland's scale, profitability and ability to woo top partners. That is difficult to do: Kirkland churns through partners at an astonishing rate. This year so far, the firm has added 119 new U.S. partners from outside the firm and lost 224, according to SurePoint.

Part of the reason Kirkland cycles through so many partners is that it pioneered the nonequity-partner tier, in which midcareer lawyers can use the title but don't own a share of the firm. These partners come and go more regularly than those with a financial stake. Most of the top firms now have this type of partner.
Overall head count is also key in the current environment because it allows firms to market themselves to large corporations as a kind of one-stop shop for their legal needs around the globe.
Decline of the white-shoe model

The New York law firms that sat atop the legal world for a century traditionally stayed intentionally small, eschewed hiring partners from other firms and relied on decadeslong relationships with institutional clients.

Historically, it was almost unheard of for a partner to leave elite firms like Cravath or Wachtell for a rival, but some high-profile recent departures have punctured that invulnerability. A few of the traditional firms, such as Davis Polk and Simpson Thacher, already changed their models years ago to look more like the megafirms, both losing and adding partners at a faster clip.
Wind down at Weil Gotshal

The war over legal talent claimed its most high-profile victim when Weil Gotshal, a 1,200-lawyer firm with a healthy balance sheet, decided to shut down. The rapid downfall was catalyzed by key partners deciding to leave the firm and served as a warning shot for other firms that such losses can quickly snowball into an existential event.
